records.transcript:
Daniel,

Thank you for your detailed response and for carrying out the further
searches.

I appreciate your confirmation that searches have been undertaken across
the available operating systems, including customer registration and
billing records and records relating to site visits and supply adjustments
or alterations.

Your response does, however, raise some further questions which I would be
grateful if you could clarify.

Most importantly, you state that following the migration to the current
billing systems in 2015:

“historical call notes, emails, webforms and other communications that may
previously have been associated with a customer or property account, were
not transferred and are therefore no longer available through our current
operating systems.”

This appears to establish that historical records of precisely the type I
am seeking may previously have existed, but were not migrated to the
current systems.

I am therefore not asking Welsh Water to speculate about what happened in
1988. I am asking whether there is any surviving documentary record
concerning the historical records themselves and their subsequent disposal
or migration.

Could you please clarify the following:

   1. *Pre-2015 records*

Were records relating to Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough held on any
legacy customer, property, works, engineering or billing system before the
2015 migration?

   2. *2015 migration*

Were historical records excluded from migration because they had already
reached their retention period, or were they excluded irrespective of their
age?

In particular, was there a defined cut-off date or retention rule
determining which historic property/account records were migrated?

   3. *Disposal*

If historic records relating to the property were destroyed or deleted
rather than migrated, is there any surviving disposal schedule, destruction
log, system-retirement record, data migration specification, audit record
or other documentation showing what categories of historical records were
removed?

   4. *Property records*

You state that you have been unable to identify surviving archived indexes,
work orders, engineer reports or other records relating to the property.

Could you please confirm whether these categories of records were
historically maintained separately from the customer billing/account
system, and whether searches were made for legacy engineering or works
records using the property name, rather than solely a modern customer
account number?

   5. *1988 supply alteration/disconnection*

I am particularly interested in whether the records show any historic
supply alteration, disconnection, meter removal, site visit, engineer
attendance, works order or instruction concerning Great House Farm during
1987–1989.

If no such records survive, please confirm whether this means:

a) no such record was ever created;
b) such records were created but subsequently destroyed under the
applicable retention policy; or
c) it is impossible to determine which of those possibilities applies
because the relevant historic records are no longer available.

   6. *Historical property/account identifiers*

If your systems retain any historic property reference, account number,
supply point reference, meter reference, works reference or other
identifier associated with Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), I would be grateful
if you could provide it. Even if the underlying records no longer survive,
such an identifier could assist in tracing the historic record elsewhere.

   7. *Records predating the current systems*

Finally, could you please confirm whether Dŵr Cymru/Welsh Water has any
central archive, historical records repository or retained legacy data from
before the 2015 system migration, and whether the searches undertaken
included those holdings?

I appreciate your statement that you cannot confirm what happened in 1988
where no records remain. I am not asking you to make such a determination
without evidence.

Rather, I am trying to establish the documentary chain: whether a record
existed, where it was held, whether it survived the transition to the
current systems, and, if not, what happened to it.

Your response has provided useful information in that respect, particularly
the confirmation that historical communications associated with
property/customer accounts were not transferred during the 2015 migration.

I would therefore be grateful if the above points could be answered so that
I can accurately record the extent and limitations of the surviving Welsh
Water records.

With regard to the £20 Guaranteed Standards Scheme payment, thank you. I am
happy to provide a forwarding address for that separately if required;
acceptance of that payment should not be taken as resolving or withdrawing
my substantive request for clarification concerning the historical records.

Regards,


Requester

Alexis Brito / Glamorgan Archives Team,

Thank you for your email (ref 2026–3941) on ACA/8/2. I note the £60 quote
for 53 images and will revert separately on that copy.

This email lists only questions I have already asked which remain
unanswered. It excludes records a family researcher has already seen by
family members at Leckwith.

Already seen, and not requested again:
- D160/1–4 as produced (Neath/Aberdare tithe maps — not the Lambert
Williams–Bute agreements)
- DSA/6/701, DSA/6/1158, booklet marked “255” / GD/LA/15/255 (Cowbridge
farm)
- DCO/WHS/2 (Cowbridge memoir)
- 6 November 1877 counterpart, Bute trustees to John Williams, Plan N5,
plus the proposed-houses plans
- Penarth poor-rate 1872–77, history-society calendars, Nancy Buckler
manuscript notes

For each item: held (ref) / not held / held elsewhere / refused. I am in
Patagonia. If held, say whether a digital copy can be supplied and at what
cost.

**26 May 2026 (2026/2370)**
1. 1974 demolition petition, Llandough juxta Penarth — ref or not held.

**29 May 2026 FOIA/EIR (2026/2372)**

2. Williams/Buckler as owners, tenants, or reporters of the 1880 floor
discovery.

3. Gaps / missing volumes / withdrawals 1950–1989.

4. Why the fabric was not scheduled before 1988 (or “Cadw holds this; we
hold nothing”).

5. Internal preservation assessments.
6. Planning files for this acreage / demolition / Church View Close — file
refs, not class names.

7. When the known archaeology was raised in planning.

8. EIAs / HER / developer briefs 1980–1990.

**27 July / 5 August 2026 (2026/3309)**
9. DB/E/1–2 Stewart survey / Cedfin.

10. Lambert Williams–Bute agreements 1818–1835 (not the D160 maps already
seen).

11. Material related to NLW D219.

12. D153/4–8 1876 limeworks severance — not seen.

13. DXJF/64/27–32 full sketch bundle — notes seen; confirm sketches and
refs.

14. DCOWHS on Buckler of Penarth (not DCO/WHS/2).

15. Exact ref of the Nov 1877 counterpart already photographed; separate
July 1877 counterpart?

16. Cardiff RDC records for this farm.

17. DRA 418–420 / DRA 5/31 if this site.

18. UDPE/S/1/68.

Glamorgan Archives Team,

I am writing to make a targeted archive research enquiry concerning the DBDT collection and any related Bute, Mountjoy or Western Ground Rents material held by Glamorgan Archives.

I am investigating the historic title, occupation and parcel boundaries of Great House Farm (Tŷ Mawr), Llandough, particularly evidence concerning a possible historical division of the farm between land retained by the Bute Estate and land allegedly sold or transferred to Daniel Thomas.

A family witness account describes a specific arrangement under which approximately ten acres, including the farmhouse, were allegedly sold by the Bute Estate to Daniel Thomas, while a separate portion of approximately nine acres remained under the Bute Estate. The account further describes quarrying on the Thomas-held land and an agreement under which the freehold would eventually pass to the occupying family when quarrying ceased.

I appreciate that this account requires verification against the original documentary record. I am therefore seeking to identify the relevant deeds, agreements, plans and subsequent title documents.

1. Verification of specific DBDT catalogue entries

Please confirm the exact property description, parties and date of the following catalogue entries, and, if possible, provide a digital copy or scan of the opening parties clause and any attached or marginal plan:

  *   DBDT10/19 – Lease (counterpart), described in the catalogue as concerning land and messuages in Bute Street, Cardiff, from trustees of the late Marquess of Bute to Mr Daniel Thomas, October 1850.
  *   DBDT10/20 – Agreement for a building lease of premises in Bute Town, Cardiff, involving the same parties, June 1849.

I understand from the catalogue descriptions that these items concern Cardiff rather than Llandough. My purpose is to establish whether the Daniel Thomas named in these instruments can be identified sufficiently to determine whether he is the same individual later connected with the Llandough lime works and land interests, or whether these are unrelated transactions involving another person of the same name.

Please also advise whether either document contains information identifying Daniel Thomas by residence, occupation, estate, trusteeship or other distinguishing details.

2. Targeted search for a Bute–Daniel Thomas transaction at or near Llandough

Please search the catalogue descriptions and indexes available to Glamorgan Archives for any deed, conveyance, exchange, sale, transfer, lease, agreement, plan or related instrument involving:

  *   Daniel Thomas;
  *   Alfred Thomas;
  *   the Marquess of Bute;
  *   trustees of the Marquess of Bute;
  *   the Bute Estate;

and land at or near:

  *   Llandough;
  *   Great House Farm / Great House / Tŷ Mawr;
  *   adjoining land or parcels that may subsequently have formed part of the farm.

I am particularly interested in transactions dating from approximately 1876 to 1878, but would be grateful for references to earlier or later documents where they form part of the same chain of title.

In particular, I am seeking evidence capable of confirming or disproving whether any defined parcel of land was conveyed by the Bute Estate to Daniel Thomas.

3. Quarrying, lime works and any conditional reversion or transfer

Please identify any relevant records concerning land at Llandough or Great House Farm that refer to:

  *   quarrying;
  *   quarries or quarry land;
  *   lime works or lime kilns;
  *   mineral rights;
  *   removal of quarrying machinery;
  *   reduction or cessation of rent as land was quarried;
  *   termination of quarrying;
  *   a future conveyance, reversion, surrender or transfer of a freehold interest when quarrying ceased.

The particular issue I am investigating is whether an agreement existed under which occupation or ownership of a defined parcel was intended to change when quarrying operations came to an end.

4. Daniel Thomas, Alfred Thomas and the Llandough lime works

Please identify any documents linking Daniel Thomas, or his son Alfred Thomas (later Lord Pontypridd), with:

  *   land at Llandough;
  *   the Llandough lime works or lime kilns;
  *   quarrying operations;
  *   Great House Farm or adjoining agricultural land;
  *   any freehold or leasehold interest in the area.

I would be particularly interested in estate papers, correspondence, conveyances, wills, probate-related estate records, rentals, rent books, abstracts of title and plans that may trace what became of any Daniel Thomas interest after his death or thereafter.

5. Subsequent title and occupation

Please identify any abstracts of title, estate maps, conveyances, correspondence, tenancy records or other material that may assist in establishing:

  1.  what happened to any freehold interest held by Daniel Thomas or his estate;
  2.  whether such an interest was ever conveyed, surrendered or transferred back to the Bute Estate or another party;
  3.  whether the Bute Estate later reacquired any relevant parcel;
  4.  whether later parties, including Mountjoy Ltd or Western Ground Rents Ltd, acquired title to land previously held by Daniel Thomas or his successors;
  5.  the basis on which later tenancies described as covering the "whole" of Great House Farm were granted.

I am also interested in any material linking these title questions with the occupation of the farm by the Williams family.

6. Plans and parcel boundaries

A separate line of research concerns the possibility that historic legal boundaries passed through or between different parts of the Great House Farm complex.

Accordingly, please identify any:

  *   estate maps;
  *   conveyance plans;
  *   tenancy plans;
  *   quarry plans;
  *   large-scale plans;
  *   boundary plans;
  *   valuation plans;

that show Great House Farm, the farmhouse, garden, stables, outbuildings or adjoining parcels.

I am particularly interested in documents that could establish whether different parts of the historic building complex fell within different legal parcels.

I appreciate that some of these requests may require staff research beyond a standard enquiry. My immediate priority is to obtain the relevant catalogue references and confirmation of what material exists. If more detailed searching or document retrieval is necessary, please let me know the applicable procedure, estimated cost and whether a formal paid research request would be required.

If relevant documents have been digitised, I would be grateful for details of the cost of obtaining copies. Otherwise, please advise whether they can be consulted in person and whether any restrictions or advance ordering requirements apply.

Thank you for your assistance. The documents identified through this enquiry may be important to reconstructing the historical chain of title and occupation of Great House Farm, Llandough from the nineteenth century onwards.

Yours faithfully,

Louise,

Thanks for your detailed and prompt reply and for the additional
information concerning the Bute Estate records and D696.

I just want to clarify one important point in relation to my original
enquiry, as I think I may have caused a slight misunderstanding about the
particular transaction I am trying to establish.

My principal question is *not whether there are deeds between the Bute
Estate and Alfred Thomas*. The key transaction I am trying to locate and
verify is the *1877 transaction concerning Daniel Thomas and the Bute
Estate*, which I understand from the surviving family evidence to have
concerned a defined portion of Great House Farm, including the farmhouse
and surrounding land. I see an 1877 agreement between both parties, for
that year, but for a different property in Cardiff. I wondered if it was
mis labelled and if you could validify its content, particularly any map
data. So as the integrity of the descriptor of the record is assured or
revisited.

The issue is whether the Bute Estate *conveyed, granted or otherwise dealt
with that defined parcel in favour of Daniel Thomas*, and, crucially, what
the instrument and its plan actually show about the boundaries and the
nature of the interest created. In 1877.

This is important because the present documentary reconstruction I am
preparing treats the 1877 instrument as the potential starting point for
the separate House Plot chain. The working case is that the instrument
dealt with the farmhouse land separately from the eastern
agricultural/quarrying parcel, with provisions connected to quarrying and
the subsequent passing of the house land to the occupying Williams family
when quarrying ceased. That proposition is expressly being treated as a
matter requiring verification against the original instrument and plan,
rather than as an established fact.

I therefore wonder whether the catalogue search could be reconsidered
specifically on the following basis:

*Bute Estate → Daniel Thomas → defined land at Llandough / Great House
Farm, approximately 1876–1878*

including instruments which may not themselves be catalogued under “Great
House Farm” or “Daniel Thomas”, but which might appear under:

   - the name of the property or former field name;
   - the Marquess of Bute or his trustees as grantor;
   - Daniel Thomas as builder, quarryman, lime-burner or occupier;
   - a lease, conveyance, agreement, surrender or counterpart;
   - quarrying or mineral rights;
   - a plan accompanying an instrument;
   - or a transaction recorded in a Bute Estate rental, ledger or estate
   correspondence rather than in the deed catalogue.

I appreciate that your catalogue may simply contain no surviving record of
this transaction. If that is the position, that is useful information in
itself. What I am particularly trying to establish is whether *the 1877
transaction has been positively searched for and not found*, as opposed to
there being no later catalogue entry linking Daniel or Alfred Thomas to the
Bute Estate.
D696 and the later Western Ground Rents material

Thank you also for pointing me towards D696. Please do let me know which
item(s) within D696 contain the *book plans and rental books for Western
Ground Rents Ltd c.1938–1944*, particularly anything relating to Great
House Farm, Llandough or the land occupied by John Williams.

This is potentially very relevant because the documentary issue I am
investigating is whether the later WGR estate corresponded geographically
with the parcel dealt with by the Bute Estate in 1877, or instead with the
separate agricultural/quarrying parcel.
Bute Estate finding aid

I would also be grateful if you could retain my enquiry against the Bute
Estate material being transferred from Cardiff Library. In particular, I
would be interested in any items concerning:

   - Llandough / Great House Farm / Tŷ Mawr;
   - Daniel Thomas;
   - the 1870s Bute Estate conveyances or leases;
   - estate plans showing parcel boundaries;
   - quarrying or lime works;
   - rentals distinguishing the farm from the farmhouse/cottages; and
   - subsequent dealings with the relevant parcels.

1910 Land Valuation map

Finally, thank you for identifying DVAL/1/33. If Glamorgan Archives has any
information enabling me to identify the corresponding *1910 valuation map
held by The National Archives*, I would be grateful for the relevant
reference. I am trying to make a targeted request rather than simply asking
The National Archives to search broadly for a Llandough map.

Thank you again for your assistance. The clarification regarding what is
and is not held at Glamorgan Archives is useful, and I appreciate your help
in narrowing down the surviving documentary trail.

Yours sincerely,

*Requester *
**

National Monuments Record / FOI Officer,

This is a request under the Freedom of Information Act 2000 and, so far as
the records concern the historic environment, the Environmental Information
Regulations 2004.

I request copies of recorded information held by RCAHMW / the National
Monuments Record of Wales relating to a reported discovery of ironwork or
“armour” under the rear wing of Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough, Vale
of Glamorgan (approx. ST 1681 7331; SMR / HER GGAT02038s; NMR NPRN
associated with Great House Farm).

The published citations which identify RCAHMW as the source, and which
state that the objects are at the National Museum of Wales, are:

1. RCAHMW, December 1988 — “Unpublished Records relating to Great House
Farm prepared by R F Suggett, December 1988.” This is the source cited in
the Glamorgan-Gwent Archaeological Trust assessment lodged on planning
application 89/01396/OUT (and carried into 92/00671/RES):

   “it is likely that some medieval ironwork which is held by the National
Museum of Wales was discovered under the rear wing c 1880 (RCAHMW 1988).”

   Bibliography: RCAHMW 1988 = Unpublished Records relating to Great House
Farm prepared by R F Suggett, December 1988.
   (GGAT, Land at Great House Farm, Llandough: An Archaeological
Assessment, August 1990.)

2. The same statement is repeated in Holbrook & Thomas, “An Early-medieval
Monastic Cemetery at Llandough, Glamorgan”, Medieval Archaeology 49 (2005),
p. 70 n. 142:

   “Mention should also be made of the fact that medieval ironwork was
discovered under the rear wing of Great House Farm c. 1880. It is now in
the collections of the National Museums & Galleries of Wales.”

3. The Heneb / Archwilio HER entry for Great House Farm (GGAT02038s)
records armour / medieval ironwork found under the rear-wing floor c.1880
and attributes the note to RCAHMW.

Please therefore provide:

A. The full text of R F Suggett’s December 1988 unpublished records
relating to Great House Farm, including every page or card that mentions
ironwork, armour, a visor, a lance, a helmet, a burial, a soldier, a horse,
a museum, or a find under the floor or rear wing / dairy.

B. Any earlier NMR / RCAHMW survey notes, correspondence or drawings that
Suggett was using (including H. J. Thomas’s 1974 survey of the house,
updated December 1988), insofar as they mention the c.1880 find or the
destination of the objects.

C. Any record of the source of Suggett’s statement that the ironwork “is
held by the National Museum of Wales” — for example a letter, accession
note, conversation record, or museum catalogue reference.

D. Any later NMR / Coflein / correspondence file that confirms, corrects or
withdraws that museum attribution.

E. File references, NPRNs and any copy letters sent to or received from the
National Museum of Wales / Amgueddfa Cymru, GGAT, Cadw or the Vale of
Glamorgan concerning this find.

I am not asking for advice or for a new interpretation. I am asking for the
recorded information that underpins the 1988 sentence now cited as fact in
the planning file and in Medieval Archaeology.

Please supply electronic copies where held. If any item is already
published on Coflein, a catalogue link and reference is enough.

Regards,

Requester

National Monuments Record / FOI Officer,

This is a request under the Freedom of Information Act 2000 and, so far as the records concern the historic environment, the Environmental Information Regulations 2004.

I request copies of recorded information held by RCAHMW / the National Monuments Record of Wales relating to a reported discovery of ironwork or “armour” under the rear wing of Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough, Vale of Glamorgan (approx. ST 1681 7331; SMR / HER GGAT02038s; NMR NPRN associated with Great House Farm).

The published citations which identify RCAHMW as the source, and which state that the objects are at the National Museum of Wales, are:

1. RCAHMW, December 1988 — “Unpublished Records relating to Great House Farm prepared by R F Suggett, December 1988.” This is the source cited in the Glamorgan-Gwent Archaeological Trust assessment lodged on planning application 89/01396/OUT (and carried into 92/00671/RES):

   “it is likely that some medieval ironwork which is held by the National Museum of Wales was discovered under the rear wing c 1880 (RCAHMW 1988).”

   Bibliography: RCAHMW 1988 = Unpublished Records relating to Great House Farm prepared by R F Suggett, December 1988.
   (GGAT, Land at Great House Farm, Llandough: An Archaeological Assessment, August 1990.)

2. The same statement is repeated in Holbrook & Thomas, “An Early-medieval Monastic Cemetery at Llandough, Glamorgan”, Medieval Archaeology 49 (2005), p. 70 n. 142:

   “Mention should also be made of the fact that medieval ironwork was discovered under the rear wing of Great House Farm c. 1880. It is now in the collections of the National Museums & Galleries of Wales.”

3. The Heneb / Archwilio HER entry for Great House Farm (GGAT02038s) records armour / medieval ironwork found under the rear-wing floor c.1880 and attributes the note to RCAHMW.

Please therefore provide:

A. The full text of R F Suggett’s December 1988 unpublished records relating to Great House Farm, including every page or card that mentions ironwork, armour, a visor, a lance, a helmet, a burial, a soldier, a horse, a museum, or a find under the floor or rear wing / dairy.

B. Any earlier NMR / RCAHMW survey notes, correspondence or drawings that Suggett was using (including H. J. Thomas’s 1974 survey of the house, updated December 1988), insofar as they mention the c.1880 find or the destination of the objects.

C. Any record of the source of Suggett’s statement that the ironwork “is held by the National Museum of Wales” — for example a letter, accession note, conversation record, or museum catalogue reference.

D. Any later NMR / Coflein / correspondence file that confirms, corrects or withdraws that museum attribution.

E. File references, NPRNs and any copy letters sent to or received from the National Museum of Wales / Amgueddfa Cymru, GGAT, Cadw or the Vale of Glamorgan concerning this find.

I am not asking for advice or for a new interpretation. I am asking for the recorded information that underpins the 1988 sentence now cited as fact in the planning file and in Medieval Archaeology.

Please supply electronic copies where held. If any item is already published on Coflein, a catalogue link and reference is enough.

Regards,

Requester

Dear Requester

Thank you for your request for information about Llandough Primary School and your further enquires around whom you within the Information Governance team you have been corresponding with.

You asked

Under the Freedom of Information Act 2000 and, where applicable, the Environmental Information Regulations 2004, I request copies of records relating to the acquisition of the land used for the construction of Llandough Primary School.

Specifically, I request:

■ The transfer deed, conveyance or other legal instrument by which the Council acquired the land.

■ The purchase price or consideration paid for the land.

■ If the land was gifted, transferred at nominal value or below market value, records explaining the basis for that arrangement.

■ Any valuation reports obtained before acquisition.

■ Any agreements, correspondence or meeting minutes between the Council and BP (or any BP subsidiary, trust or associated company) concerning the transfer of the land.

■ Any Cabinet, Committee or Council reports authorising the acquisition.

■ Any planning agreements or obligations connected with the transfer.

If any of the requested information is already publicly available, please provide the relevant links or document references.

You then issued further correspondence requesting:

On 14 July 2026 you acknowledged my FOI/EIR request (Case Ref 00211027) concerning the acquisition of land for Llandough Primary School.

I replied the same day asking for the name of the officer who sent the acknowledgement. I have received no further response or substantive reply.

Our Response

The transfer deed, conveyance or other legal instrument by which the Council acquired the land
The Council holds a conveyance dated 11 June 1965 made between:
1.            Lakeside and Llandough Development Company Limited;
2.            Western Ground Rents Limited; and
3.            The Glamorgan County Council.
A scanned copy of the conveyance and its plan is attached (“the 1965 Conveyance”).

The purchase price or consideration paid for the land
The consideration recorded in the 1965 Conveyance is £16,800.

If the land was gifted, transferred at nominal value or below market value, records explaining the basis of that arrangement
The 1965 Conveyance records a purchase for £16,800. No record has been located within the papers held by Legal Services indicating that the land was gifted or transferred at nominal value or below market value.

Any valuation reports obtained before acquisition
Searches were undertaken with Legal Services and Estates Department. No valuation report relating to the acquisition has been identified. The Council does not hold any valuation report falling within the scope of this request.

Any agreements, correspondence or meeting minutes between the Council and BP, or any BP subsidiary, trust or associated company, concerning the transfer
No agreements, correspondence or meeting minutes between the Council and BP or any BP subsidiary, trust or associated company relating to the acquisition of the land have been identified.

Any Cabinet, Committee or Council reports authorising the acquisition
The Council has not identified any Cabinet, Committee or Council reports within its current records management systems which fall within the scope of your request. Given the age of the acquisition, any surviving historic records may have been transferred to Glamorgan Archives. You may wish to contact Glamorgan Archives directly regarding records from this period.

Any planning agreements or obligations connected with the transfer
No planning agreement or planning obligation connected with the 1965 Conveyance has been identified within the title deeds held by Legal Services or, within the Planning Departments records.

The requests are dealt with via a generic e-mail account so that all officers in the Team can consider correspondence.  There are several reasons why the Information Governance Team work in this way.  One reason is to ensure that correspondence is considered as soon as possible and to ensure that messages or e-mails are not sent to individuals and overlooked within our systems overall. Royal Commission,

I am researching the demolition of Great House Farm (Tŷ Mawr),
Llandough-juxta-Penarth, in December 1988 (HER reference GGAT02038s / ST
1681 7331).

I am seeking to establish whether the Royal Commission was consulted or
notified before the farmhouse was demolished.

Contemporary reports from 3 December 1988 state that Cadw was considering
emergency protection/listing of Great House Farm and that a Cadw inspection
was being arranged, including discussion with the Royal Commission for
Ancient and Historical Monuments.

The farmhouse was then demolished on 6 December 1988.

I understand that the statutory framework at the time included provisions
concerning the recording of historic buildings before authorised
demolition. I would therefore be grateful if you could check your records
and confirm:

   1.

   Whether the Royal Commission received any notification, consultation,
   referral or request for advice concerning Great House Farm before its
   demolition in December 1988.
   2.

   Whether the Royal Commission was asked to inspect, photograph, record or
   otherwise document the building before demolition.
   3.

   Whether any correspondence exists between the Royal Commission, Cadw,
   the local planning authority, BP Properties Ltd, or their representatives
   concerning the proposed demolition.
   4.

   Whether the Royal Commission was given an opportunity to complete or
   supplement its earlier recording of the farmhouse before demolition.
   5.

   Whether your records contain any photographs, measured drawings,
   reports, field notes or other documentation relating specifically to the
   farmhouse immediately before its demolition.
   6.

   If records exist, I would be grateful for the relevant reference numbers
   and, where possible, copies.

For context, the Royal Commission had already recorded Great House Farm
architecturally in 1974. Contemporary material indicates that the building
was subsequently under consideration for emergency listing shortly before
its destruction.

There is also an important chronology concerning the occupation and
possession of the property: my late father William Buckler had lodged
European Commission of Human Rights application 14464/88 on 3 May 1988; BP
obtained possession on 29 November 1988; demolition began on 6 December
1988; and the Strasbourg application was registered on 12 December 1988.

I am not asking the Royal Commission to express an opinion on the ownership
dispute or the legality of the demolition. I am simply seeking to
establish, from your records, whether the Commission was notified or
consulted and what opportunity, if any, it was given to record the building
(our home since 1667) before it was destroyed?

Given the historical and archaeological significance subsequently
identified at the site, I would particularly appreciate confirmation of
whether any pre-demolition recording was requested or undertaken.

Regards


,

Customer Relations / Planning Complaints Officer,

I wish to make a formal complaint concerning the Vale of Glamorgan
Council's Dear Customer Relations / Planning Complaints Officer,

I wish to make a formal complaint concerning the Vale of Glamorgan
Council's handling of Great House Farm, Llandough-juxta-Penarth,
particularly the circumstances surrounding its demolition in December 1988
and the subsequent planning process.


Please register this as a formal complaint under the Council's corporate
complaints procedure and provide me with a complaint reference number.


This complaint concerns the Council's administration and exercise of its
planning and heritage responsibilities. It is not intended to constitute an
appeal against a properly made historic planning decision.


1. Great House Farm, Llandough (Cardiff not Cowbridge) was recognised as a
building of historic importance


The planning and archaeological documentation concerning the site
identifies Great House Farm as a building of heritage significance.


In particular, the archaeological material identifies the former building
as a "county treasure" associated with SMR 2038s, while earlier
architectural recording by RCAHMW describes a substantial historic
farmhouse with surviving historic fabric.


The later 1990 archaeological assessment states:


«"Owing to an ownership dispute and the subsequent sudden destruction of
the property in 1988 the building was incompletely understood."»


I regard that statement as highly significant because it records,
contemporaneously with the subsequent planning process, that the building
had been destroyed suddenly and that its archaeological and architectural
history had therefore not been adequately understood or recorded.


2. The Council's apparent failure to take protective action before the 1988
demolition


I ask the Council to investigate what action, if any, its planning and
heritage officers took when Great House Farm was at risk of demolition.


In particular, I ask the Council to establish:


1. Whether the Council knew that Great House Farm was at risk of demolition
before December 1988.

2. Whether the Council received any notification, complaint, application,
correspondence or other warning concerning the proposed demolition.

3. Whether the building had been considered for statutory listing or other
statutory protection.

4. Whether consideration was given to the use of a Building Preservation
Notice or any other available statutory or administrative mechanism capable
of preventing or delaying demolition pending assessment.

5. Whether the Council's heritage officers, planning officers or
archaeological advisers were consulted.

6. Whether any inspection or photographic/architectural record was
undertaken immediately before or after the demolition.

7. Why, given the building's recognised historic significance, the Council
did not secure a comprehensive standing-building record before the building
was lost.


I am not asserting at this stage that a particular statutory power
necessarily had to be exercised. I am asking the Council to investigate
what powers and procedures were available in 1988 and why they were, or
were not, used in this case.


3. The "sudden destruction" of the building requires investigation


The 1990 archaeological assessment expressly attributes the incomplete
understanding of the building to its "subsequent sudden destruction ... in
1988".


I therefore ask the Council to establish from its records:


- the date on which it first became aware of the proposed or actual
demolition;

- the identity of the relevant officers;

- whether the Council received complaints or reports concerning demolition
activity;

- whether any site visit took place;

- whether any notice, warning, enforcement action, preservation action or
other intervention was considered;

- and whether the Council has retained records explaining why the
demolition was allowed to proceed.


This is particularly important because the building was subsequently
treated within the planning process as an already-cleared site.


4. The 1989 planning application appears to contain a significant
historical discrepancy


The outline planning application submitted by BP Properties Ltd in 1989
states, in the section asking which buildings were to be demolished:


«"None."»


The same application describes the site as "Disused" and the previous use
as "Not known".


This requires explanation because the application followed the demolition
of Great House Farm in December 1988 by approximately one year.


I ask the Council to investigate whether its planning officers:


- were aware of the former Great House Farm building when the 1989
application was processed;

- knew when and how it had been demolished;

- checked the accuracy of the applicant's statement that no buildings were
to be demolished;

- identified the former farmhouse in the planning history and supporting
documentation;

- and considered whether the demolition itself raised any planning,
heritage or enforcement issue requiring investigation.


I am particularly concerned that the planning process appears to have
proceeded on the basis of a cleared site without first establishing the
circumstances in which the historic building had disappeared.


5. Failure to create an adequate record of the lost building


The subsequent archaeological documentation states that the building was
"incompletely understood".


I ask the Council to explain what mitigation, recording or investigation it
required in consequence.


The documentary evidence presently available indicates that substantial
historic fabric and multiple phases of the building existed, yet the
building was destroyed without a complete standing-building survey having
been secured.


I therefore ask the Council to identify:


- all surveys undertaken before demolition;

- all surveys undertaken after demolition;

- all archaeological or architectural advice obtained by the Council;

- all photographs held by the Council;

- all correspondence concerning the building's architectural or historic
importance;

- and the Council's policy or practice in 1988 concerning the recording of
significant unlisted historic buildings at risk.


6. Subsequent planning treatment of the site


Following demolition, the planning process concentrated heavily on
below-ground archaeology, ultimately resulting in archaeological
investigation of the cemetery and associated remains.


I do not suggest that archaeological excavation was inappropriate. My
concern is that the destruction of the standing historic building appears
to have been treated as a fait accompli rather than as an event requiring
accountability and an explanation of how the Council's heritage
responsibilities had been discharged.


The later planning documentation should therefore be reviewed alongside the
records relating to the 1988 demolition.


In particular, I ask the Council to identify precisely when the planning
authority first recorded the former farmhouse as demolished and what
explanation was placed on the planning file for its loss.


7. Matters I ask the Council to investigate


Please investigate and provide a substantive response to the following
questions:


A. What did Vale of Glamorgan Council know about the impending demolition
of Great House Farm before December 1988?


B. What statutory and non-statutory heritage protections were available to
the Council at the time?


C. Were any of those mechanisms considered or discussed?


D. Were any Building Preservation Notice, listing, enforcement, urgent
works, archaeological recording or other protective measures considered?


E. Why was the building apparently destroyed without a comprehensive
standing-building survey?


F. What records does the Council hold concerning the demolition itself?


G. Why did the 1989 planning application proceed despite the recent
demolition of a building identified in the archaeological record as a
"county treasure"?


H. Why was the applicant's answer "None" given to the question concerning
buildings to be demolished, and did the Council investigate the apparent
discrepancy?


I. Did any Council officer consider whether the 1988 demolition constituted
a breach of planning control or otherwise required investigation?


J. Did the Council investigate whether the building had been demolished
lawfully?


K. What heritage assessment was undertaken before the subsequent
development permissions were processed?


L. What lessons has the Council subsequently incorporated into its
procedures for County Treasures and other locally significant historic
buildings?


8. Records requested as part of the investigation


Please preserve and review all relevant records, including planning files,
enforcement records, heritage files, committee papers, officer reports,
internal correspondence, site inspection notes, photographs, archaeological
correspondence and consultation records concerning:


- Great House Farm / Tŷ Mawr / Cedfin / Cydfin;

- SMR/HER reference 2038s / GGAT02038s;

- the December 1988 demolition;

- the 1989 outline planning application;

- the 1990 archaeological assessment;

- and the subsequent reserved matters/development applications.


I would also ask that the Council identify any material which has been
destroyed or cannot now be located, together with the applicable
retention/disposal record where one exists.


9. Outcome sought


I am seeking a formal investigation and a reasoned written explanation of
the Council's actions and omissions.


In particular, I ask the Council to determine:


1. Whether its officers discharged the heritage and planning
responsibilities applicable at the time.

2. Whether any failure occurred in relation to the identification,
protection, recording or investigation of Great House Farm.

3. Whether the Council's handling of the 1989 planning application
appropriately addressed the recent demolition of the building.

4. Whether any relevant records have been lost or destroyed and, if so,
when and under what retention arrangements.

5. What procedural lessons arise from the case.


I also request disclosure of the relevant non-exempt records identified
during the complaint investigation, where these are not otherwise
available. I recognise that requests for specific recorded information may
need to be dealt with separately under the appropriate information-access
regime.


I have only recently been able to examine and correlate the surviving
planning, archaeological and heritage documentation sufficiently to
identify these issues. I therefore ask that the Council accepts the
complaint for investigation notwithstanding the age of the events concerned.


Please acknowledge receipt and confirm the complaint reference and the
officer responsible for its investigation.


Yours faithfully,

   or other intervention was considered;
   - and whether the Council has retained records explaining why the
   demolition was allowed to proceed.

This is particularly important because the building was subsequently
treated within the planning process as an already-cleared site.
4. The 1989 planning application appears to contain a significant
historical discrepancy

The outline planning application submitted by BP Properties Ltd in 1989
states, in the section asking which buildings were to be demolished:

"None."

The same application describes the site as "Disused" and the previous use
as "Not known".

This requires explanation because the application followed the demolition
of Great House Farm in December 1988 by approximately one year.

I ask the Council to investigate whether its planning officers:

   - were aware of the former Great House Farm building when the 1989
   application was processed;
   - knew when and how it had been demolished;
   - checked the accuracy of the applicant's statement that no buildings
   were to be demolished;
   - identified the former farmhouse in the planning history and supporting
   documentation;
   - and considered whether the demolition itself raised any planning,
   heritage or enforcement issue requiring investigation.

I am particularly concerned that the planning process appears to have
proceeded on the basis of a cleared site without first establishing the
circumstances in which the historic building had disappeared.
5. Failure to create an adequate record of the lost building

The subsequent archaeological documentation states that the building was
"incompletely understood".

I ask the Council to explain what mitigation, recording or investigation it
required in consequence.

The documentary evidence presently available indicates that substantial
historic fabric and multiple phases of the building existed, yet the
building was destroyed without a complete standing-building survey having
been secured.

I therefore ask the Council to identify:

   - all surveys undertaken before demolition;
   - all surveys undertaken after demolition;
   - all archaeological or architectural advice obtained by the Council;
   - all photographs held by the Council;
   - all correspondence concerning the building's architectural or historic
   importance;
   - and the Council's policy or practice in 1988 concerning the recording
   of significant unlisted historic buildings at risk.

6. Subsequent planning treatment of the site

Following demolition, the planning process concentrated heavily on
below-ground archaeology, ultimately resulting in archaeological
investigation of the cemetery and associated remains.

I do not suggest that archaeological excavation was inappropriate. My
concern is that the destruction of the standing historic building appears
to have been treated as a fait accompli rather than as an event requiring
accountability and an explanation of how the Council's heritage
responsibilities had been discharged.

The later planning documentation should therefore be reviewed alongside the
records relating to the 1988 demolition.

In particular, I ask the Council to identify precisely when the planning
authority first recorded the former farmhouse as demolished and what
explanation was placed on the planning file for its loss.
7. Matters I ask the Council to investigate

Please investigate and provide a substantive response to the following
questions:

A. What did Vale of Glamorgan Council know about the impending demolition
of Great House Farm before December 1988?

B. What statutory and non-statutory heritage protections were available to
the Council at the time?

C. Were any of those mechanisms considered or discussed?

D. Were any Building Preservation Notice, listing, enforcement, urgent
works, archaeological recording or other protective measures considered?

E. Why was the building apparently destroyed without a comprehensive
standing-building survey?

F. What records does the Council hold concerning the demolition itself?

G. Why did the 1989 planning application proceed despite the recent
demolition of a building identified in the archaeological record as a
"county treasure"?

H. Why was the applicant's answer "None" given to the question concerning
buildings to be demolished, and did the Council investigate the apparent
discrepancy?

I. Did any Council officer consider whether the 1988 demolition constituted
a breach of planning control or otherwise required investigation?

J. Did the Council investigate whether the building had been demolished
lawfully?

K. What heritage assessment was undertaken before the subsequent
development permissions were processed?

L. What lessons has the Council subsequently incorporated into its
procedures for County Treasures and other locally significant historic
buildings?
8. Records requested as part of the investigation

Please preserve and review all relevant records, including planning files,
enforcement records, heritage files, committee papers, officer reports,
internal correspondence, site inspection notes, photographs, archaeological
correspondence and consultation records concerning:

   - Great House Farm / Tŷ Mawr / Cedfin / Cydfin;
   - SMR/HER reference 2038s / GGAT02038s;
   - the December 1988 demolition;
   - the 1989 outline planning application;
   - the 1990 archaeological assessment;
   - and the subsequent reserved matters/development applications.

I would also ask that the Council identify any material which has been
destroyed or cannot now be located, together with the applicable
retention/disposal record where one exists.
9. Outcome sought

I am seeking a formal investigation and a reasoned written explanation of
the Council's actions and omissions.

In particular, I ask the Council to determine:

   1. Whether its officers discharged the heritage and planning
   responsibilities applicable at the time.
   2. Whether any failure occurred in relation to the identification,
   protection, recording or investigation of Great House Farm.
   3. Whether the Council's handling of the 1989 planning application
   appropriately addressed the recent demolition of the building.
   4. Whether any relevant records have been lost or destroyed and, if so,
   when and under what retention arrangements.
   5. What procedural lessons arise from the case.

I also request disclosure of the relevant non-exempt records identified
during the complaint investigation, where these are not otherwise
available. I recognise that requests for specific recorded information may
need to be dealt with separately under the appropriate information-access
regime.

I have only recently been able to examine and correlate the surviving
planning, archaeological and heritage documentation sufficiently to
identify these issues. I therefore ask that the Council accepts the
complaint for investigation notwithstanding the age of the events concerned.

Please acknowledge receipt and confirm the complaint reference and the
officer responsible for its investigation.

Yours faithfully,




Requester

Royal Commission,

I am researching the demolition of Great House Farm (Tŷ Mawr), Llandough-juxta-Penarth, in December 1988 (HER reference GGAT02038s / ST 1681 7331).

I am seeking to establish whether the Royal Commission was consulted or notified before the farmhouse was demolished.

Contemporary reports from 3 December 1988 state that Cadw was considering emergency protection/listing of Great House Farm and that a Cadw inspection was being arranged, including discussion with the Royal Commission for Ancient and Historical Monuments.

The farmhouse was then demolished on 6 December 1988.

I understand that the statutory framework at the time included provisions concerning the recording of historic buildings before authorised demolition. I would therefore be grateful if you could check your records and confirm:

  1.  Whether the Royal Commission received any notification, consultation, referral or request for advice concerning Great House Farm before its demolition in December 1988.
  2.  Whether the Royal Commission was asked to inspect, photograph, record or otherwise document the building before demolition.

  6.  If records exist, I would be grateful for the relevant reference numbers and, where possible, copies.

For context, the Royal Commission had already recorded Great House Farm architecturally in 1974. Contemporary material indicates that the building was subsequently under consideration for emergency listing shortly before its destruction.

There is also an important chronology concerning the occupation and possession of the property: my late father William Buckler had lodged European Commission of Human Rights application 14464/88 on 3 May 1988; BP obtained possession on 29 November 1988; demolition began on 6 December 1988; and the Strasbourg application was registered on 12 December 1988.

I am simply seeking to establish, from your records, whether the Commission was notified or consulted and what opportunity, if any, it was given to record the building (our home since 1667) before it was destroyed?
